newsitem.title: USA: Europeans battle to allay euro fears at G7 summit.
newsitem.headline: Europeans battle to allay euro fears at G7 summit.

text.p: European leaders at the Group of Seven summit in Denver told their global partners with a single voice -- the euro is coming, it will be on time, it will be a success and it will not throw financial markets into disarray.

The summit's brief discussions on the euro, the planned single currency which will form the focus of Europe's 1999 economic and monetary union (EMU), were summed up in a single paragraph in the final economic statement.

"We discussed EMU, including its international implications. We welcome the efforts of European countries to achieve a successful introduction of the euro and a well-functioning EMU, underpinned by sound macroeconomic and structural policies, that would contribute to the stability of the international monetary system," the statement said.

Comments from the Europeans went even further, brushing aside any weakness in the language of the statement to make clear the euro should be treated as a fact of life -- 18 months before its inception -- with no chance now for a delay.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl told reporters that there could be no question that EMU would start as planned in 1999, despite the problems many European countries are facing in meeting the economic targets to qualify for EMU entry.
"I have never doubted this...My (G7) colleagues are in absolutely no doubt about this," Kohl said.
European Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said the comment was typical of the stance of European leaders and finance ministers at the meeting.
"There was a unanimous determination from the Europeans to say that the euro will be launched on January 1, 1999," de Silguy said. "It's a done deal".

The Group of Seven is made up of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. Representatives of the European Union and the Netherlands, which currently has the presidency of the EU also attended the Denver, Colorado talks.

The continental Europeans -- Germany, France, Italy and the European Union officials -- went out of their way to stress that other countries' fears that a failed euro could create turmoil on financial markets had been put to rest.
"The previous skepticism is no longer there," German economics minister Guenter Rexrodt said.

Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said: "It is beyond doubt that the United States looks favorably on the creation of a single currency in which a broad group of countries participate, which gives stability to the monetary situation."
And even British Prime Minister Tony Blair, whose country sits on the fence on the merits of the single currency, made the point that the planned euro had to be strong.
"We cannot have...a Europe that has a single currency that is a weak currency,' he told ABC television.

But the non-Europeans among the G7 group signalled nonetheless that they remained quietly skeptical, sending out the between-the-lines message that while there was no external opposition to Europe's currency plans, the currency had better live up to everyone's expectations.
One senior U.S. official commented, "We're concerned that the EMU debate not divert Europe from structural reform, fiscal reform and EU enlargement."
A Japanese spokesman said Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto had warned fellow G7 leaders on Saturday that EMU should "proceed in a stable manner".
"When the single currency is born, it is important that a strong EMU be created," the spokesman said.
A senior Canadian official was more direct. "It is simple. We want a successful euro because we don't want them to screw up the financial markets," he told reporters.
